questions.question: Why is implementing Runnable preferred over extending Thread in Java?
questions.title: Runnable Preferred Over Thread Extension
questions.direct_answer: Implementing **Runnable** is preferred because: (1) Java doesn't support multiple inheritance — extending Thread blocks you from extending another class; (2) Runnable separates the **task** from the **thread**, allowing reuse; (3) Runnable works with ExecutorService and thread pools, Thread does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of OOP design and thread management best practices
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Just saying 'Runnable is better' without giving the three reasons
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the single inheritance limitation and the task-vs-thread separation principle

sections.title: Three Reasons Runnable is Preferred
sections.content:
**Reason 1: Single inheritance**
Java classes can only extend one class. If you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class. Implementing Runnable leaves inheritance free for your domain hierarchy.

**Reason 2: Separation of concerns**
Runnable represents a **task** (what to do). Thread represents a **thread** (the mechanism). Separating them allows the same task to be run differently — in a new Thread, in a thread pool, or even synchronously.

**Reason 3: Works with ExecutorService**
ExecutorService.execute(Runnable) and submit(Runnable) accept Runnable. You cannot submit a Thread subclass the same way.

sections.title: Task Reuse Across Mechanisms
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: There are three solid reasons. First, Java only allows single inheritance — if you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class. That severely limits your design options. Second, it's better object-oriented design: a Runnable represents the task itself, while a Thread is just the execution mechanism. Keeping them separate means the same task can be submitted to a thread pool, run in a new Thread, or even called synchronously in tests. Third, Runnable integrates with ExecutorService — you submit Runnables and Callables to executor services, which is how production Java handles threading. Extending Thread doesn't plug into that ecosystem.

questions.question: What is the difference between Runnable and Callable in Java?
questions.title: Runnable vs Callable in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Runnable** has `run()` that returns **void** and cannot throw checked exceptions. **Callable<V>** has `call()` that returns **a value** of type V and can throw checked exceptions. Use Callable when you need a result or to throw checked exceptions from a thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of both task interfaces and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Callable can throw checked exceptions — a key feature over Runnable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the Future.get() pattern for getting Callable results

sections.title: Runnable vs Callable
sections.content:
| Aspect | Runnable | Callable<V> |
|---|---|---|
| Method name | run() | call() |
| Return type | void | V (generic type) |
| Checked exceptions | Cannot throw | Can throw |
| Used with | Thread, executor.execute() | executor.submit() |
| Returns | Nothing | Future<V> |
| Available since | Java 1.0 | Java 5 |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Runnable's run() returns void and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable's call() returns a generic value and can throw checked exceptions. When you submit a Callable to an ExecutorService, you get back a Future. Future.get() blocks until the result is ready. If the Callable threw an exception, Future.get() wraps it in an ExecutionException. Callable is the right choice when your background task produces a result you need back, or when it might throw a checked exception like IOException. Runnable is fine for fire-and-forget tasks where you don't need a result.

followup_questions: What happens when you call Future.get() and the Callable threw an exception?
Can you use a Callable with a raw Thread?

groups.heading: Runnable
groups.text: Has run() — returns void, can't throw checked exceptions. Used for fire-and-forget tasks. Works with raw Thread, executor.execute(), or executor.submit() (which returns a Future<?> where get() returns null).

groups.heading: Callable<V>
groups.text: Has call() — returns a value of type V and can throw checked exceptions. Only works with executor.submit(), which returns Future<V>. Call future.get() to block and retrieve the result, or future.get(timeout) to not wait forever.

items: Use Runnable for background jobs with no result needed — sending a notification, updating an audit log.
Use Callable when the task produces a value you need — fetching external data, computing a price.

beats.text: In the order app: a Callable that queries a shipping API and returns the shipping cost. You submit it, do other order preparation, then call future.get() to get the cost and complete the order total calculation.

speakable_v2.cap: When your background task needs to hand something back, Callable is the answer — Runnable is just for side effects.

questions.question: If Runnable is preferred, when would you ever extend Thread?
questions.title: When to Extend Thread Instead of Implementing Runnable
questions.direct_answer: You extend Thread when you need to **modify Thread behavior itself** — like overriding `start()` logic or accessing Thread methods directly. In practice, this is rare in application code. Most production code uses Runnable with ExecutorService.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate gives a thoughtful answer or just says 'you never should'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'you never extend Thread' — there are legitimate but rare cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Acknowledge the pattern is rare and explain the specific use case

sections.title: Rare Cases for Extending Thread
sections.content:
Legitimate cases for extending Thread:

1. **Framework/library code** that creates specialized Thread subclasses with extra behavior (e.g., custom `start()` pre-processing, thread-specific context storage)

2. **Testing** — creating a specialized thread with tracking capabilities

3. **Naming and grouping** — when you need convenient access to thread-specific metadata without passing it separately

However, **in application code**, extending Thread is almost never necessary. Modern Java uses Runnable/Callable with ExecutorService, and thread-local context is handled via `ThreadLocal<T>` — not by subclassing Thread.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The honest answer is that extending Thread is rarely necessary in application code. The main legitimate use case is when you're building a framework or library and you genuinely need to modify Thread behavior itself — like overriding start() to do some pre-processing, or adding monitoring capabilities to every thread. Application developers almost never need this. If you need thread-specific context, use ThreadLocal. If you need task results, use Callable with ExecutorService. Extending Thread for regular task execution is an older pattern that predates the Executor framework, and modern code doesn't need it.

questions.question: What is ThreadLocal in Java and when would you use it?
questions.title: ThreadLocal in Java
questions.direct_answer: **ThreadLocal** gives each thread its **own isolated copy** of a variable. Changes made by one thread don't affect other threads. It's used for per-thread context like user sessions, database connections, or date formatters that are not thread-safe.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows about per-thread state — used in Spring Security and request contexts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that ThreadLocal values must be removed (or cause memory leaks in thread pools)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring's RequestContextHolder and SecurityContextHolder as real-world ThreadLocal uses

sections.title: ThreadLocal Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- Each thread gets its own isolated copy via ThreadLocal
- Spring Security stores the authenticated user in SecurityContextHolder (ThreadLocal-backed)
- SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe — ThreadLocal is a classic solution
- In thread pools: threads are reused, so always call remove() after each task
- Memory leak risk: if you forget remove(), old values linger as threads are reused
- Java's InheritableThreadLocal allows child threads to inherit parent's values

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own private copy of a variable. Thread A and Thread B can both call get() and set() on the same ThreadLocal object, but they see completely independent values. The classic use case is SimpleDateFormat, which is not thread-safe — you can store one instance per thread using ThreadLocal instead of synchronizing. In Spring, SecurityContextHolder uses ThreadLocal to store the authenticated user for the current request's thread. One important gotcha: in thread pools, threads are reused across tasks. If you don't call remove() after your task completes, the old value is still in the thread when it picks up the next task. This can cause security bugs or weird behavior.

followup_questions: What is SecurityContextHolder and how does it use ThreadLocal?
What happens if you don't remove a ThreadLocal value in a thread pool?

beats.text: ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own completely independent copy of a variable. Thread A and Thread B both call get() and set() on the same ThreadLocal object, but they see different values. No synchronization needed — they can never interfere with each other.

Some objects are not thread-safe but are expensive to create — like SimpleDateFormat. Instead of synchronizing access to a shared one, you give each thread its own via ThreadLocal. Spring Security uses this pattern to store the authenticated user without passing it through every method signature.

items: set(value): stores a value for the current thread only.
get(): retrieves the current thread's value — completely isolated from other threads.
remove(): clears the value for the current thread — critical in thread pools.

beats.text: production trap: In your order app using a thread pool, thread reuse means old ThreadLocal values persist into the next request. If you don't call remove() after handling each request, Thread A's user context might leak into the next request Tomcat assigns to that thread — a serious security bug.

items: Always call remove() after each task in a thread pool — otherwise old values leak into reused threads.
Don't store large objects in ThreadLocal — each thread gets its own copy, multiplying memory usage.

speakable_v2.cap: ThreadLocal is elegant for per-thread context, but the remove() discipline in thread pools is non-negotiable.

questions.question: How does the Runnable interface relate to lambda expressions?
questions.title: Runnable as a Functional Interface
questions.direct_answer: **Runnable** is a **functional interface** — it has exactly one abstract method (`run()`). Since Java 8, any functional interface can be implemented with a **lambda expression**. This means any lambda that takes no arguments and returns void is a valid Runnable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connection between multithreading knowledge and Java 8 features
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not connecting Runnable to the functional interface concept
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how method references also work as Runnable implementations

sections.title: Runnable with Lambda and Method Reference
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Runnable is a functional interface — it has just one abstract method, run(). In Java 8, any functional interface can be implemented with a lambda. Since run() takes no arguments and returns void, any zero-argument lambda that doesn't return anything is automatically a Runnable. That's why you can write new Thread(() -> doSomething()) and it works — the lambda IS the Runnable. Method references work too: if you have a static void method somewhere, you can use a method reference as a Runnable. This is one of the clearest examples of how Java 8 lambdas eliminated boilerplate in multithreading code.

beats.text: A functional interface is any interface with exactly one abstract method. Java 8 introduced lambdas that can implement any functional interface. Runnable has one abstract method — run() with no parameters and void return. So any lambda with no parameters and no return value is automatically a Runnable.

Before Java 8, every Runnable needed an anonymous class — five lines of boilerplate for what's essentially one line of logic. Lambda support for Runnable eliminated this friction, making thread creation far less verbose.

items: Lambda as Runnable: () -> doWork() — the compiler infers the type from context.
Method reference as Runnable: OrderProcessor::processNext — static or instance method with matching signature.
@FunctionalInterface annotation: optional on Runnable, confirms it's meant to be a functional interface.

beats.text: non-obvious: The lambda captures outer variables, but they must be effectively final. In a for loop creating multiple threads, capturing the loop variable 'i' fails unless you copy it first: final int taskId = i. This is a very common mistake for freshers writing parallel processing loops.

items: Loop variables must be effectively final before capturing in a lambda — copy them first.
Lambdas capture by reference for objects, not by value — changes to the captured object are visible inside the lambda.

speakable_v2.cap: Runnable as a functional interface is one of Java 8's clearest wins — it made threading code dramatically more readable overnight.

questions.question: Can a Runnable be passed to both Thread and ExecutorService?
questions.title: Runnable Compatibility with Thread and ExecutorService
questions.direct_answer: Yes. **Runnable is accepted by both** `new Thread(runnable)` and `ExecutorService.execute(runnable)` / `submit(runnable)`. This is the key design advantage — the same task definition works with different execution mechanisms.

interviewer_intent.testing: Confirmation that the candidate understands Runnable's versatility
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing ExecutorService also accepts Runnable — thinking it only takes Callable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between execute() (returns void) and submit() (returns Future)

sections.title: Runnable Across Mechanisms
Key Points
sections.content:
- Runnable works with: Thread constructor, ExecutorService.execute(), ExecutorService.submit()
- execute() returns void — fire and forget
- submit(Runnable) returns Future<?> — can wait for completion but result is null
- Same Runnable object can be submitted multiple times
- This flexibility is why Runnable is the universal task interface in Java

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, the same Runnable works with both. That's actually the main design advantage of Runnable over extending Thread. You can pass it to new Thread(), to executor.execute(), or to executor.submit(). The submit() version returns a Future, but since Runnable has no return value, calling Future.get() returns null — it's mainly useful to wait for task completion. execute() just fires and forgets. So Runnable really is the universal task interface in Java — define your task once, run it however you need.

speakable_v2.hook: The same Runnable works with both raw Thread and ExecutorService — that's the whole point of separating the task from the threading mechanism.

beats.text: Runnable is accepted by new Thread(runnable), ExecutorService.execute(runnable), and ExecutorService.submit(runnable). All three run the same task. The difference is execution context — a new OS thread, a pooled thread — but the Runnable definition is identical.

This versatility is the core design advantage of Runnable over Thread extension. Define your task once, run it anywhere — in tests synchronously, in production with a thread pool, with a single thread or hundreds.

items: execute(runnable): fire-and-forget, returns void.
submit(runnable): returns Future<?> — get() returns null but lets you wait for completion.
new Thread(runnable).start(): one-off thread outside any pool.

beats.text: sharp edge: submit(runnable) returns a Future<?>, but future.get() always returns null for a Runnable. The only reason to use submit() over execute() for a Runnable is to be able to call future.get() to wait for the task to complete or to catch exceptions that the task threw.

items: Exceptions thrown inside a Runnable submitted via execute() are silently swallowed — use submit() and check the Future to catch them.
Don't mix execute() and submit() carelessly — know whether you need the Future or not.

speakable_v2.cap: Runnable's compatibility with both Thread and ExecutorService is the reason it's the universal task interface in Java.
